prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian prose oeuvre, rooted in poetry, that builds expansive inner cosmologies from memory, the body and dream.

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged, and the reasons are literary, not the shape of the round-1 record. Public knowledge of Blinding and Solenoid points to a recognizable voice and to books that are constructed, with recurring image systems and nested structures, so that scale does real formal work. Memory, the body and dream are treated as one metaphysical enterprise. This is the clearest combination on the list of distinctiveness, formal ambition and imaginative depth, and it is judged across decades, not on a single peak. The oeuvre looks consolidated, since the late major novels continue and enlarge the earlier project, so premature judgment is not my concern. After the exchange I have changed the citation wording. Carlberg's argument and the chair's question persuaded me that the citation should rest on the prose, the part of the corpus we can weigh most honestly, and name poetry as the root of the project and not as an independently assessed pillar. That wording is more accurate to my evidence. It also keeps the citation to one writer and one prize part and does not depend on national or European symbolism or a period label.
statement.case_against: The case still depends on dense, rhythmic Romanian prose that I can judge only through translation, and I have not independently verified the corpus. Architecture and excess can look alike in very long forms. I cannot show from the evidence in front of me that the later volumes deepen the earlier image systems and do not merely recirculate them, which is Palm's test and the chair's first question. If a reader of the originals or of Romanian-language criticism showed that the late novels mainly repeat the earlier ones, the claim of sustained quality across the whole body of work would weaken and my first preference would be open. The poetry and early work are also thinner in translation, so the claim of one coherent oeuvre across genres is partly inferred.

responses.point: Carlberg would anchor a Cărtărescu citation on the novels, with poetry as an origin of the vision and not as an independently assessed pillar, because translated coverage of the poetry is thin.
responses.response: I accept this and have changed my citation. My round-1 wording named prose and poetry jointly, which claimed more than I can weigh. The revised wording names the prose oeuvre and says it is rooted in poetry. That treats the poetry as a hypothesis about origin, as Mattson also puts it, and not as an established pillar. On Carson I agree with your scope point, and I see no reason to move her above the preferred candidate. I am keeping her as my first alternative because her voice and formal invention are distinctive, not because of a count of colleagues.

responses.point: Palm proposes a test for Cărtărescu and Can Xue alike: is the consistency of method a deepening or only a repetition? She sees a visible arc from the poetry through the Blinding sequence to Solenoid, and says she cannot judge whether such an arc exists for Can Xue.
responses.response: I accept the test and want it applied evenly. Public knowledge suggests the Blinding trilogy has a deliberate large-scale design, and that Solenoid moves toward a different, more essayistic and intellectually driven register. That is an inference from reputation, not a reading I can verify, and it is why I regard the arc as plausible but unproven. It is a reasonable basis for a preference, not a demonstration. I would revisit the case if a reader of the Romanian showed that the late work only restates the earlier imagery. Applying the same test to Can Xue is why I still cannot place her higher. The question is open for her, not answered against her.

responses.point: Olsson reads Can Xue's decades-long consistency of method as sustained distinctiveness, where I read it as a question about development. He also holds that Michon's sentence-level achievement is very high but that significance across a body of work is the sticking point.
responses.response: I accept that consistency can be distinctiveness, and I should not have made it the main ground for ranking her last among my eight. My reservation is evidentiary: I cannot tell from a partial translated corpus whether the method changes in ways that matter. I would not say she lacks development, only that I cannot confirm it. On Michon we are close. We agree on the sentence-level achievement and differ on how far a compact oeuvre limits significance. I read the size as a limit on how widely the case can be tested, not on the quality of the work. Since the style is so bound to French syntax, I keep him as an alternative and not as a first choice.

responses.point: Swärd says that if the committee valued formal reinvention of a language or genre over expansion of an established visionary mode, Tawada or Adonis would have a stronger claim than Cărtărescu.
responses.response: That is a real difference in weighting, and I do not dismiss it. I would resist the premise that Cărtărescu only expands a mode. Building a whole cosmology out of memory and the body at that scale is a formal invention of its own, even when it draws on a visionary lineage. I agree that reinvention of a language is a legitimate criterion. For Adonis and Tawada the difficulty remains that I cannot test the case without the original languages. If colleagues who can read Arabic, Japanese or German said which works carry the case, that could move my alternatives, but I have no such evidence now. I therefore leave them off my list of two alternatives.

responses.point: Mattson treats the claim that poetry is the base of Cărtărescu's prose project as the part of the case she can least verify, and says it should be held as a hypothesis. She also asks whether Carson's short or fragmentary work carries enough cumulative weight.
responses.response: I agree on the poetry, and it is the second reason for the citation change above. On Carson, I think the weight question and the design-dependence question are linked. Some of her strongest books depend on physical form, which I cannot assess, and a citation limited to the written poetry and essays would be narrower than the work that made her reputation. A Carson citation could still be defined, but it would be less self-evident than the Cărtărescu one. That is why I keep her second, behind the preferred candidate, and why the Cărtărescu citation need not claim more than the prose can support.

uncertainties: How well the density and rhythm of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose carry in translation, and whether the longest books deepen their image systems or recirculate them. I cannot settle this from public knowledge.
Translation coverage of the poetry and early work is thin, so the 'rooted in poetry' clause of the citation is an inference, and the citation is deliberately anchored on the prose.
Whether Can Xue's consistent method reflects depth or limited variation, given a partial translated corpus.
How much of Adonis's standing rests on the poems themselves as against historical influence, since I cannot assess the Arabic originals.
Whether Carson's hybrid and book-object works fit the will's conception of the literary work, and whether a citation can be defined around her original written work alone.

I would not prefer no award (P000): the shared public record of Cărtărescu's major work seems sufficient for a recommendation, though I have not read the corpus for this exercise or independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I find no documented tie between me and any shortlisted writer in the supplied profile. The documented connections are collegial and institutional: election alongside Ingrid Carlberg in 2020, service with the other listed members, and long ties to the SvD and DN culture sections and the Prague and Vienna literary milieus. My own Central European subject matter is context only and is not evidence of a preference for any candidate. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
